agree.reason: Opening on traffic as a neighbour who lives with the morning backup, and asking for the signal as a binding condition, gives the two traffic-minded commissioners a reason to vote yes; opposing neighbours get little beyond that, because the parking-sharing offer and the construction liaison commitment are missing.

honest.reason: The numbers are accurate, but saying 'the traffic gets handled' claims more than the study does: the signal keeps one intersection at a C, while 310 more trips still use Alder, and Margaret said she can't promise traffic won't get worse; 'working people, seniors, and families' is also an added description.

works_the_facts.reason: The facts are listed correctly but barely worked: the speech never says the 64 homes could house about one in six of the 412 waiting households, and it never points out the 8 spare parking spaces or what 310 trips means per hour at rush hour.

right_comparison.reason: It names the alternative fairly (an empty lot six days a week while 412 households wait an average of three years), but it doesn't say the shortage and the wait continue or grow if this project is turned down.

qualification.reason: Making the signal a permit condition is concrete and checkable, and it names the C-versus-D result, but there is no timing (for example, signal in place before occupancy) and no consequence if the signal isn't built.

objections.reason: It deals with the intersection rating, but it leaves out the 20 months of construction trucks on Alder, the written offer to share the lot for neighbour parking, and Margaret's place on the construction neighbour group, all of which answer objections the opposing neighbours will raise.

fit.reason: At about 400 words of plain, spoken first-person text with a clear ask at the start and end, it fits within the three-minute limit.
